claim: Sleep deprivation shifts food choices toward energy-dense options.
source: Sleep deprivation has marked effects on food intake, shifting food choices toward energy-dense options.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known effect and is supported by experimental data in the results section showing increased energy density of food consumed after sleep deprivation.

claim: Sleep restriction increased levels of 2-oleoylglycerol (2-OG).
source: We found that sleep restriction increased levels of the ECS compound 2-oleoylglycerol (2-OG)
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sleep restriction enhanced encoding of food odors in piriform cortex.
source: We found that sleep restriction increased levels of the ECS compound 2-oleoylglycerol (2-OG), enhanced encoding of food odors in piriform cortex
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by MVPA decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The relationship between changes in 2-OG and food choices was formally mediated by odor-evoked connectivity between the piriform cortex and insula.
source: Importantly, the relationship between changes in 2-OG and food choices was formally mediated by odor-evoked connectivity between the piriform cortex and insula, a region involved in integrating feeding-related signals.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by mediation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When individuals are sleep-deprived, their dietary behavior shifts toward increased consumption of foods high in sugar and fat, leading to weight gain.
source: When individuals are sleep-deprived, their dietary behavior shifts toward increased consumption of foods high in sugar and fat, leading to weight gain (Markwald et al., 2013; Nedeltcheva et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Effects of sleep deprivation on ingestive behavior are likely related to sleep-dependent changes in appetite-regulating compounds, including ghrelin, leptin, and endocannabinoids.
source: These effects on ingestive behavior are likely related to sleep-dependent changes in appetite-regulating compounds, including ghrelin (Rihm et al., 2019; Spiegel et al., 2004b), leptin (Spiegel et al., 2004a), and endocannabinoids (Hanlon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The endocannabinoid system (ECS) exerts strong effects on food intake.
source: Indeed, the endocannabinoid system (ECS) exerts strong effects on food intake (Bellocchio et al., 2010; Di Marzo et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Levels of the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) and its structural analog 2-oleoylglycerol (2-OG) are enhanced in sleep-deprived individuals.
source: levels of the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) and its structural analog 2-oleoylglycerol (2-OG) are enhanced in sleep-deprived individuals (Hanlon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The neural pathways through which sleep-dependent alterations in the ECS influence food intake have not been investigated in humans.
source: While previous studies have tested the effects of sleep deprivation on the human brain (Greer et al., 2013; Krause et al., 2017; Muto et al., 2016; Rihm et al., 2019), the neural pathways through which sleep-dependent alterations in the ECS influence food intake have not been investigated in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature, supported by citations showing what has been studied.

claim: Odors serve as powerful signals for the initiation and termination of feeding behavior.
source: Odors serve as powerful signals for the initiation and termination of feeding behavior (Saper et al., 2002; Shepherd, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Animal studies have shown that olfactory processing is modulated in a state-dependent manner.
source: animal studies have shown that olfactory processing is modulated in a state-dependent manner (Julliard et al., 2007; McIntyre et al., 2017; Murakami et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: In rodents and humans, olfaction is altered by hunger and satiety.
source: In rodents (Aimé et al., 2007; Aimé et al., 2014) and humans (Hanci and Altun, 2016; Stafford and Welbeck, 2011), olfaction is altered by hunger and satiety
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in both rodents and humans.

claim: Satiety reduces neural activity in olfactory brain regions in parallel with a suppression of feeding behavior.
source: satiety reduces neural activity in olfactory brain regions in parallel with a suppression of feeding behavior (Boesveldt, 2017; Gervais and Pager, 1979; O'Doherty et al., 2000; Prud'homme et al., 2009; Soria-Gómez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent work across different species suggests a link between the ECS, olfactory processing, and food intake.
source: Moreover, recent work across different species suggests a link between the ECS, olfactory processing, and food intake, such that endocannabinoids may directly modulate neural activity in olfactory circuits (Breunig et al., 2010; Soria-Gómez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Endocannabinoids may directly modulate neural activity in olfactory circuits.
source: such that endocannabinoids may directly modulate neural activity in olfactory circuits (Breunig et al., 2010; Soria-Gómez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies, with speculative language ('may').

claim: Whether odor-evoked responses in the human olfactory system are modulated by the ECS, and whether this accounts for the effects of sleep deprivation on food intake, is not known.
source: However, whether odor-evoked responses in the human olfactory system are similarly modulated by the ECS, and whether this accounts for the effects of sleep deprivation on food intake, is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The insula integrates olfactory, gustatory, homeostatic, and visceral signals.
source: Olfactory, gustatory, homeostatic, and visceral signals are integrated in the insula (Craig, 2002; de Araujo et al., 2003; Johnson et al., 2000; Livneh et al., 2017; Small et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The insula is optimally positioned to regulate ingestive behavior in a state-dependent manner.
source: optimally positioning this region to regulate ingestive behavior in a state-dependent manner (Dagher, 2012; de Araujo et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and logical inference from its integrative role.

claim: The study included 25 healthy-weight participants (10 male, mean age 26.6 ± 0.98 years).
source: healthy-weight participants (N = 25, 10 male, age mean ± SEM: 26.6 ± 0.98 years)
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Actigraphy-monitored sleep times did not differ between DS and NDS sessions during the 7-nights of sleep stabilization.
source: Actigraphy-monitored sleep times did not differ between DS and NDS sessions during the 7-nights of sleep stabilization (NDS: 6.63 ± 0.18 hr, DS: 6.75 ± 0.19 hr; T22=−1.40, p=0.174).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of actigraphy data.

claim: Sleep times differed significantly during the night of sleep manipulation between DS and NDS sessions.
source: However, sleep times did differ during the night of sleep manipulation (NDS: 6.8 ± 0.12 hr, DS: 3.8 ± 0.18 hr; T24 = 14.70, p=1.68×10−13, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of actigraphy data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Subjects complied with the sleep deprivation protocol.
source: confirming that subjects complied with the sleep deprivation protocol.
evidence: Inferred from the significant difference in sleep times during manipulation.

claim: In the DS compared to the NDS session, participants reported lower sleep quality.
source: In the DS compared to the NDS session, participants reported lower sleep quality (DS 2.96 ± 0.19, NDS 3.96 ± 0.18, T22=−3.98, p=6.38×10−4)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of self-report data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the DS compared to the NDS session, participants reported reduced alertness.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of self-report data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the DS compared to the NDS session, participants felt less well-rested.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of self-report data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Stanford Sleepiness Scale scores were higher in the DS session compared to NDS.
source: Stanford Sleepiness Scale scores were higher in the DS session (DS 3.64 ± 0.24, NDS 2.08 ± 0.19, T24 = 6.96, p=3.40×10−7).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There were no significant changes in State Anxiety Inventory scores between DS and NDS sessions.
source: There were no significant changes in SAI scores (T24=−1.49, p=0.148)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no significant changes in cortisol levels between DS and NDS sessions.
source: or cortisol (T24 = 0.70, p=0.584) between DS and NDS sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stress and anxiety levels were not altered by sleep restriction.
source: suggesting that stress and anxiety levels were not altered by sleep restriction.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant changes in SAI scores and cortisol levels.

claim: There were no sleep-dependent differences in hunger ratings at any time point.
source: Importantly, there were no sleep-dependent differences in hunger ratings made at any time point
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of hunger ratings shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Measures of odor-evoked brain activity and food intake cannot be driven by differences in subjective levels of hunger.
source: indicating that measures of odor-evoked brain activity and food intake cannot be driven by differences in subjective levels of hunger.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of sleep-dependent differences in hunger ratings.

claim: There were no sleep-dependent differences in rated odor pleasantness and intensity during fMRI scanning.
source: There were no sleep-dependent differences in rated odor pleasantness and intensity, or respiratory behavior during fMRI scanning (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: There were no sleep-dependent differences in respiratory behavior during fMRI scanning.
source: There were no sleep-dependent differences in rated odor pleasantness and intensity, or respiratory behavior during fMRI scanning (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the DS session, participants consumed food items with a significantly higher energy density.
source: In the DS session, participants consumed food items with a significantly higher energy density (6.0 ± 2.43% change from NDS; T24 = 2.48, p=0.021, Figure 1F)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of buffet food intake shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There was no significant difference in the overall calories consumed between DS and NDS sessions at the post-scan buffet.
source: with no significant difference in the overall calories consumed (18.6 ± 16.93% change from NDS; T24 = 1.10, p=0.282).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of buffet food intake.

claim: Effects of sleep deprivation on dietary behavior persisted into the next day, with a higher percentage of calories consumed as fat.
source: Importantly, effects of sleep deprivation on dietary behavior persisted into the next day (after a night of unrestricted recovery sleep), with a higher percentage of calories consumed as fat (DS: 36.5 ± 1.28%, NDS: 30.6 ± 1.28%; T24 = 2.34, p=0.028)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of next-day food diary data.

claim: A single night of restricted sleep can have relatively long-lasting effects on food choices.
source: indicating that a single night of restricted sleep can have relatively long-lasting effects on food choices.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of effects into the next day.

claim: Circulating levels of 2-OG collected during fMRI scanning were increased in the DS relative to the NDS session.
source: Partially replicating the previous findings, circulating levels of 2-OG collected during fMRI scanning were increased in the DS relative to the NDS session (35.02 ± 17.82% change from NDS; T24 = 1.96, p=0.031, one-tailed, Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of blood samples shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sleep-dependent changes in 2-AG and 2-OG were significantly correlated.
source: Although sleep-dependent changes in 2-AG and 2-OG were significantly correlated (r = 0.55, p=0.004)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of blood sample data.

claim: Relative increases in 2-AG were not significant between DS and NDS sessions.
source: relative increases in 2-AG were not significant (5.29 ± 5.20% change from NDS; T24 = 1.02, p=0.16, one-tailed).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of blood samples.

claim: No significant changes were observed in ghrelin, leptin, and insulin between DS and NDS sessions.
source: We also observed no significant changes in other appetite-regulating hormones, including ghrelin, leptin, and insulin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Sleep-dependent increases in 2-OG correlated significantly with increases in the energy density of food consumed at the post-scanning buffet.
source: Interestingly, sleep-dependent increases in 2-OG correlated significantly with increases in the energy density of food consumed at the post-scanning buffet (robust regression, β = 0.47, p=0.027; permutation test, p=0.018; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by robust regression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ECS may play a role in modifying dietary behavior after sleep deprivation.
source: Although correlative in nature, this finding suggests that the ECS may play a role in modifying dietary behavior after sleep deprivation.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between 2-OG and energy-dense food choices, with speculative language.

claim: Odors are encoded in piriform cortex by sparsely distributed patterns of ensemble activity, with no apparent topographical organization.
source: Both animal (Barnes et al., 2008; Illig and Haberly, 2003; Stettler and Axel, 2009) and human studies (Howard et al., 2009; Zelano et al., 2011) have shown that odors are encoded in piriform cortex by sparsely distributed patterns of ensemble activity, with no apparent topographical organization.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous animal and human studies.

claim: Significant decoding of odor information was found in the piriform cortex across sleep sessions.
source: Across sleep sessions, we found significant decoding of odor information in the piriform cortex (x = 16, y=−2, z=−14, T24 = 4.20, PFWE-SVC = 0.012, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by MVPA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant decoding of odor information was found in the insula across sleep sessions.
source: and insula (left x=−32, y=−4, z = 16, T24 = 4.75, PFWE-SVC = 0.021; right x = 44, y = 8, z = 10, T24 = 4.84, PFWE-SVC = 0.017).
evidence: Supported by MVPA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Decoding accuracy for food vs. non-food odors in the piriform cortex was significantly higher in the DS session compared to NDS.
source: Importantly, comparing odor encoding between DS and NDS sessions, we found significantly higher decoding accuracy in the piriform cortex in the DS session (x = 20, y = 8, z=−12, T24 = 5.91, PFWE-SVC = 0.001; Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by MVPA analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sleep deprivation enhances encoding of odor information in olfactory brain areas.
source: suggesting that sleep deprivation enhances encoding of odor information in olfactory brain areas.
evidence: Inferred from the higher decoding accuracy in piriform cortex in the DS session.

claim: A univariate analysis of odor-evoked fMRI responses in piriform cortex showed no sleep-dependent effects or interactions.
source: In contrast, a univariate analysis of odor-evoked fMRI responses in piriform cortex showed no sleep-dependent effects or interactions (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by univariate analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Decoding accuracy in piriform cortex was not correlated with sleep-dependent changes in 2-OG.
source: However, decoding accuracy in piriform cortex was not correlated with either sleep-dependent changes in 2-OG (r=−0.24, p=0.248)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Decoding accuracy in piriform cortex was not correlated with energy-dense food choices.
source: or energy-dense food choices (r=−0.05, p=0.80)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The relationship between the ECS and food intake was not directly mediated by changes in odor encoding.
source: suggesting that the relationship between the ECS and food intake was not directly mediated by changes in odor encoding.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlations between decoding accuracy and 2-OG or food choices.

claim: Sleep-dependent changes in piriform connectivity with the right insula correlated with changes in the energy density of food consumed immediately after the fMRI session.
source: We found that sleep-dependent changes (DS >NDS) in piriform connectivity (odorized >clean air) with the right insula correlated with changes in the energy density of food consumed immediately after the fMRI session (x = 40, y = 6, z = 0, T23 = 6.04, PFWE-SVC = 0.005; Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by PPI analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Reduced odor-evoked connectivity between piriform cortex and insula was associated with enhanced intake of energy-dense food.
source: such that reduced odor-evoked connectivity was associated with enhanced intake of energy-dense food (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by correlation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A positive correlation was found between sleep-dependent changes in energy-dense food choices and changes in odor-evoked connectivity between the piriform cortex and the right anterior hippocampus.
source: In addition, while not part of our main set of hypotheses, we found a positive correlation between sleep-dependent changes in energy-dense food choices and changes in odor-evoked connectivity between the piriform cortex and the right anterior hippocampus (x = 28, y=−10, z=−18, T23 = 5.36, Puncorr = 1.0×10−5).
evidence: Supported by PPI analysis.

claim: Sleep-dependent changes in piriform connectivity for food vs. non-food odors did not show a significant relationship with changes in food choices.
source: In contrast, sleep-dependent changes in piriform connectivity for food vs. non-food odors did not show a significant relationship with changes in food choices.
evidence: Supported by PPI analysis.

claim: The connectivity between olfactory signals in the piriform cortex and downstream areas may play a role in linking sleep-dependent changes in olfactory processing to changes in food choices.
source: These results suggest that the connectivity between olfactory signals in the piriform cortex and downstream areas may play a role in linking sleep-dependent changes in olfactory processing to changes in food choices.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between piriform-insula connectivity and food choices, with speculative language.

claim: Piriform-insula connectivity was significantly correlated with sleep-dependent changes in 2-OG levels.
source: Indeed, we found that piriform-insula connectivity was significantly correlated with sleep-dependent changes in 2-OG levels (r=−0.58, p=0.002; Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The association between sleep-dependent changes in ECS and food choices is mediated by piriform-insula connectivity.
source: raising the possibility that the association between sleep-dependent changes in ECS and food choices is mediated by piriform-insula connectivity.
evidence: Inferred from the correlations, with speculative language, and tested with formal mediation analysis.

claim: The direct path between 2-OG levels and food intake was fully explained by the indirect path through piriform-insula connectivity, establishing a significant mediation effect.
source: Importantly, the direct path between 2-OG levels and food intake was fully explained by the indirect path through piriform-insula connectivity, establishing a significant mediation effect (Sobel test, z = 2.97, p=0.003).
evidence: Supported by formal mediation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Sleep deprivation affects the ECS, which then modulates the connectivity between piriform and insular cortex, and in turn shifts food choices toward energy-dense options.
source: This suggests that sleep deprivation affects the ECS, which then modulates the connectivity between piriform and insular cortex, and in turn shifts food choices toward energy-dense options.
evidence: Inferred from the mediation analysis results.

claim: Clinical and epidemiological studies have linked reduced sleep to elevated food intake and weight gain.
source: Clinical and epidemiological studies have linked reduced sleep to elevated food intake and weight gain (Kant and Graubard, 2014; Markwald et al., 2013; Patel and Hu, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sleep restriction increases the desire for foods high in sugar and fat content.
source: This relationship has been confirmed in studies using experimentally induced sleep deprivation, demonstrating that sleep restriction increases the desire for foods high in sugar and fat content (Cain et al., 2015; Greer et al., 2013; Hogenkamp et al., 2013; Simon et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sleep restriction leads to excessive consumption of foods high in sugar and fat.
source: and leads to excessive consumption of such food options (Brondel et al., 2010; Nedeltcheva et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous imaging studies have reported sleep-dependent activity changes in response to food cues.
source: In addition, previous imaging studies have reported sleep-dependent activity changes in response to food cues (Benedict et al., 2012; Greer et al., 2013; Rihm et al., 2019; St-Onge et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whether and how neural changes are related to actual food choices and the ECS has remained unclear.
source: but whether and how these neural changes are related to actual food choices and the ECS has remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge.

claim: Previous animal studies have established an important role for the ECS in regulating feeding behavior.
source: Previous animal studies have established an important role for the ECS in regulating feeding behavior (Bellocchio et al., 2010; Di Marzo et al., 2001; Rodríguez de Fonseca et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: 2-AG stimulates food intake and lipogenesis by activating CB1 receptors.
source: Whereas 2-AG stimulates food intake and lipogenesis by activating CB1 receptors (DiPatrizio and Simansky, 2008; Osei-Hyiaman et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The exact role of 2-OG and its relation to 2-AG is not fully understood.
source: the exact role of 2-OG and its relation to 2-AG is not fully understood (Murataeva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Sleep-dependent increases in 2-OG are associated with changes in the consumption of energy-dense foods.
source: Our study shows that sleep-dependent increases in 2-OG are associated with changes in the consumption of energy-dense foods, providing novel evidence for a link between sleep, ECS, and dietary behavior.
evidence: Supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sleep restriction induced qualitative changes in food intake, biasing choices toward energy-dense options, without altering total calorie intake.
source: We found that sleep restriction induced qualitative changes in food intake, biasing choices toward energy-dense options, without altering total calorie intake.
evidence: Supported by the data showing increased energy density but no change in total calories.

claim: Some studies have shown increases in calorie intake with sleep deprivation.
source: Although some studies have shown increases in calorie intake with sleep deprivation (Al Khatib et al., 2017; Broussard et al., 2016; Markwald et al., 2013; Patel and Hu, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The current findings are in line with several other studies showing no increase in total calorie intake.
source: our findings are in line with several other studies (Cain et al., 2015; Nedeltcheva et al., 2009; Simon et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sleep deprivation induces nuanced changes in food-based decision making, rather than simply increasing hunger or the motivation to eat.
source: and suggest that sleep deprivation induces nuanced changes in food-based decision making, rather than simply increasing hunger or the motivation to eat.
evidence: Inferred from the qualitative changes in food choices without changes in total intake or hunger ratings.

claim: Neural processing of odors is enhanced in primary olfactory brain areas after sleep restriction.
source: Our results further elaborate on the effects of sleep deprivation on the human brain, suggesting that neural processing of odors is enhanced in primary olfactory brain areas after sleep restriction.
evidence: Supported by the increased decoding accuracy in piriform cortex.

claim: Encoding of food vs. non-food odors was more robust in the piriform cortex in a sleep-deprived state.
source: Although decoding accuracy can be influenced by factors other than the strength of neural encoding, such as reduced variability (noise), our results indicate that encoding of food vs. non-food odors was more robust in the piriform cortex in a sleep-deprived state.
evidence: Inferred from the increased decoding accuracy, with acknowledgment of alternative explanations.

claim: Enhanced encoding of olfactory information could facilitate odor-evoked approach and consummatory responses.
source: In theory, such enhanced encoding of olfactory information could facilitate odor-evoked approach and consummatory responses (Aimé et al., 2007; Soria-Gómez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation supported by citations, with speculative language ('could').

claim: There was no direct correlation between encoding in piriform cortex and food intake.
source: However, we did not observe a direct correlation between encoding in piriform cortex and food intake
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Changes in odor information were not directly related to changes in circulating levels of 2-OG.
source: and changes in odor information were not directly related to changes in circulating levels of 2-OG.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Nonlinear effects or interactions among different ECS compounds may have obscured a direct linear relationship between 2-OG and encoding in piriform cortex.
source: It is possible that nonlinear effects or interactions among different ECS compounds (Ho et al., 2008; Murataeva et al., 2016) may have obscured a direct linear relationship between 2-OG and encoding in piriform cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of correlation, supported by citations.

claim: Sleep-dependent increases in odor information may not directly mediate the relationship between the ECS and food intake.
source: In any case, our findings indicate that sleep-dependent increases in odor information may not directly mediate the relationship between the ECS and food intake.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of direct correlations.

claim: Interactions between olfactory cortex and downstream areas may translate altered chemosensory encoding into changes in food intake.
source: Instead, they suggest that interactions between olfactory cortex and downstream areas may translate altered chemosensory encoding into changes in food intake.
evidence: Inferred from the mediation analysis, with speculative language ('may').

claim: Changes in piriform-insula connectivity were correlated with the effects of sleep deprivation on food choices.
source: We found that changes in piriform-insula connectivity were correlated with the effects of sleep deprivation on food choices
evidence: Supported by PPI analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a relationship between sleep-dependent food intake and neural processing in extended olfactory pathways.
source: suggesting a relationship between sleep-dependent food intake and neural processing in extended olfactory pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between piriform-insula connectivity and food choices.

claim: A formal mediation analysis showed that relative increases in 2-OG were related to reductions in odor-evoked piriform-insula connectivity, which in turn was correlated with increased choices of energy-dense food options.
source: A formal mediation analysis showed that relative increases in 2-OG were related to reductions in odor-evoked piriform-insula connectivity, which in turn was correlated with increased choices of energy-dense food options.
evidence: Supported by mediation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: These findings need to be confirmed in future studies.
source: Although these findings need to be confirmed in future studies
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the need for replication.

claim: There is a broader role for neural processing of chemosensory signals along piriform-insula pathways in the regulation of food intake.
source: they suggest a broader role for neural processing of chemosensory signals along piriform-insula pathways in the regulation of food intake.
evidence: Inferred from the mediation results, with speculative language.

claim: Sensory and visceral-homeostatic signals are integrated in the insula.
source: Previous studies show that sensory and visceral-homeostatic signals are integrated in the insula
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Integration of sensory and homeostatic signals in the insula is critical for guiding food intake.
source: and that this integration is critical for guiding food intake (de Araujo et al., 2003; Livneh et al., 2017; Small, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reduced piriform-insula connectivity could reflect a diminished integration of chemosensory and homeostatic-visceral information.
source: Reduced piriform-insula connectivity could reflect a diminished integration of chemosensory and homeostatic-visceral information
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: A failure to adequately integrate elevated olfactory signals with homeostatic information may drive excess intake of energy-dense food.
source: and a failure to adequately integrate elevated olfactory signals with homeostatic information may drive excess intake of energy-dense food.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism, with speculative language ('may').

claim: Reduced piriform-insula connectivity could indicate an aberrant assignment of value to energy-dense foods.
source: Alternatively, reduced piriform-insula connectivity could indicate an aberrant assignment of value to energy-dense foods (Balleine and Dickinson, 2000; Gottfried et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation, supported by citations.

claim: Sleep deprivation decreases activity in other cortical areas.
source: Finally, to the degree that sleep deprivation decreases activity in other cortical areas (Greer et al., 2013; Muto et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reduced piriform-insula connectivity may be related to diminished top-down control over elevated olfactory signals in piriform cortex.
source: it is possible that reduced piriform-insula connectivity is related to diminished top-down control over elevated olfactory signals in piriform cortex
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism, with speculative language ('it is possible').

claim: Diminished top-down control may promote impulsive behavior in response to energy-dense food.
source: which may promote impulsive behavior in response to energy-dense food (Cedernaes et al., 2014; Krause et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations, with speculative language ('may').

claim: The food odors were rated as higher in pleasantness than non-food odors.
source: As expected, the food odors were rated as higher in pleasantness than non-food odors.
evidence: This is an expected result based on the experimental design.

claim: It is possible that observed effects for food vs. non-food odor encoding in the brain were fully explained by pleasantness differences.
source: In principle, it is therefore possible that our observed effects for food vs. non-food odor encoding in the brain were fully explained by this corresponding pleasantness difference.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential confound.

claim: The results remained significant when including pleasantness as a covariate in the statistical models.
source: However, our results remained significant when including pleasantness as a covariate in the statistical models
evidence: This is a control analysis to rule out the confound.

claim: Pleasantness does not account for the observed results.
source: indicating that in this case pleasantness does not account for our results.
evidence: Inferred from the control analysis.

claim: Sleep-dependent changes in food choices are associated with changes in an olfactory pathway that is related to the ECS.
source: Taken together, our findings show that sleep-dependent changes in food choices are associated with changes in an olfactory pathway that is related to the ECS.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: This pathway is likely not restricted to sleep-dependent changes in food intake but may also account for dietary decisions more generally.
source: This pathway is likely not restricted to sleep-dependent changes in food intake but may also account for dietary decisions more generally.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the findings.

claim: The current findings may help to guide the identification of novel targets for treatments of obesity.
source: In this regard, our current findings may help to guide the identification of novel targets for treatments of obesity.
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings.

claim: The study included healthy, right-handed, non-smoking, and non-obese men and women between the ages of 18–40 years with BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 kg/m².
source: We consented and screened 41 healthy, right handed, non-smoking, and non-obese men and women between the ages of 18–40 year and body mass index (BMI) between 18.5 and 24.9 kg/m2
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Participants had no history of neurological disorders.
source: with no history of neurological disorders.
evidence: This is an exclusion criterion for the study.

claim: The study included individuals with a self-reported habitual sleep duration of 7–9 hours.
source: We included individuals with a self-reported habitual sleep duration of 7–9 hr
evidence: This is an inclusion criterion for the study.

claim: The study included individuals with regular sleep time between 9 pm and midnight.
source: and regular sleep time between 9 pm and midnight.
evidence: This is an inclusion criterion for the study.

claim: The 7–9 hour habitual sleep inclusion criteria was based on guidelines set by National Sleep Foundation for healthy adults.
source: The 7–9 hr habitual sleep inclusion criteria was based on guidelines set by National Sleep Foundation for healthy adults (Hirshkowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This justifies the inclusion criterion with a citation.

claim: The inclusion criteria ensured that all participants had sleep duration and sleep timing within the normal range for this age group.
source: This ensured that all participants had sleep duration and sleep timing that are within the normal range for this age group.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the inclusion criteria.

claim: A regular sleep time between 9 pm and midnight ensured circadian rhythms were aligned across all participants.
source: A regular sleep time between 9 pm and midnight ensured circadian rhythms were aligned across all participants (Burgess and Eastman, 2004), minimizing between-subject variance.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the inclusion criterion, supported by citation.

claim: The study excluded individuals with daytime nap, variable sleep habits, regular night work, travel across time zones during the study, use of medications affecting sleep, and caffeine intake of >300 mg/day.
source: Additional exclusion criteria were daytime nap, variable sleep habits, regular night work, travel across time zone during the study, use of medications affecting sleep, and caffeine intake of >300 mg/day.
evidence: These are exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Only individuals with Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale scores below 16 were included in the study.
source: We also administered the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (cut off 16) (Radloff, 1977), and the Pittsburgh Sleeping Quality Index (cut off 5) (Buysse et al., 1989). Only individuals with scores below the cut off were included in the study.
evidence: This is an inclusion criterion based on screening measures.

claim: Only individuals with Pittsburgh Sleeping Quality Index scores below 5 were included in the study.
source: We also administered the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (cut off 16) (Radloff, 1977), and the Pittsburgh Sleeping Quality Index (cut off 5) (Buysse et al., 1989). Only individuals with scores below the cut off were included in the study.
evidence: This is an inclusion criterion based on screening measures.

claim: Only non-pregnant women were included in the study.
source: Only non-pregnant women were included.
evidence: This is an exclusion criterion for the study.

claim: Of the 41 individuals screened, 29 proceeded with the experimental procedures.
source: Of the 41 individuals screened, 29 proceeded with the experimental procedures.
evidence: This describes the flow of participants through the study.

claim: Three participants dropped out of the study due to discomfort inside the scanner.
source: Of those, three participants dropped out of the study due to discomfort inside the scanner
evidence: This describes participant attrition.

claim: One participant was excluded from the analysis because of a large number of missed responses.
source: and one was excluded from the analysis because of a large number of missed responses.
evidence: This describes participant exclusion.

claim: The main outcome measures did not differ between male and female participants.
source: The main outcome measures did not differ between male and female participants (energy density: T23 = 0.618, p=0.542; 2-OG: T23=−0.826, p=0.416; piriform encoding: T23 = 0.095, p=0.924)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The main outcome measures did not correlate with body weight.
source: and did not correlate with body weight (energy density: β = 0.019, p=0.865; 2-OG: β=−1.334, p=0.103; piriform encoding: β = 0.024, p=0.611).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis.

claim: All experimental procedures of this study were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Northwestern University.
source: All experimental procedures of this study (STU00203395) were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Northwestern University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: There was a washout period of 19 days between the last day of the first session and the first day of second session.
source: There was a washout period of 19 days between the last day of the first session (7 days of sleep stabilization phase, 1 day sleep manipulation, 1 day fMRI session) and the first day of second session (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The two fMRI days were separated by 28 days for all participants.
source: This ensured that the two fMRI days were separated by 28 days for all participants
evidence: This is a consequence of the washout period design.

claim: Female participants were tested in the same phase of the menstrual cycle.
source: such that female participants were tested in the same phase of the menstrual cycle.
evidence: This is a rationale for the 28-day separation.

claim: No significant differences were found between the two menstrual phases in sleep-dependent changes in primary outcome measures.
source: In addition, we recorded self-reported menstrual cycle phase and compared sleep-dependent changes in our primary outcome measures between female participants in the follicular and luteal phase. No significant differences were found between the two menstrual phases (energy-dense food intake: T10=−0.76, p=0.465; 2-OG: T10=−1.41, p=0.188; piriform encoding: T10=−0.05, p=0.960).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Participants were instructed to maintain a standardized sleep schedule of 7–9 hours sleep between 10:30 pm and 7:30 am during the week preceding each session.
source: During the week preceding each session, participants were instructed to maintain a standardized sleep schedule of 7–9 hr sleep (between 10:30 pm and 7:30 am) in order to align the phase of the circadian rhythm across participants.
evidence: This describes the sleep stabilization protocol.

claim: Compliance with the sleep schedule during the sleep stabilization and sleep manipulation phase was monitored using wrist-worn actigraphy and a self-reported sleep diary.
source: Compliance with the sleep schedule during the sleep stabilization and sleep manipulation phase was monitored using wrist-worn actigraphy and a self-reported sleep diary.
evidence: This describes the monitoring methods.

claim: Subjects rated their subjective sleep quality, alertness, and restfulness every morning using an online questionnaire.
source: Subjects also rated their subjective sleep quality, alertness, and restfulness every morning using an online questionnaire.
evidence: This describes the subjective measures collected.

claim: No naps were allowed during both sleep stabilization and sleep manipulation periods.
source: No naps were allowed during both sleep stabilization and sleep manipulation periods.
evidence: This describes a protocol restriction.

claim: Participants were instructed to abstain from alcohol, caffeine, and drugs, including all recreational drugs, to avoid interference with sleep and hormone levels.
source: Participants were also instructed to abstain from alcohol, caffeine, and drugs, including all recreational drugs, to avoid interference with sleep and hormone levels.
evidence: This describes protocol restrictions.

claim: Participants were instructed to consume not more than one small caffeinated drink per day to ensure caffeine intake was limited to <300 mg/day on sleep stabilization days.
source: To ensure that participants limited their caffeine intake to <300 mg/day on sleep stabilization days, they were instructed to consume not more than one small caffeinated drink per day.
evidence: This describes the caffeine restriction protocol.

claim: Subjects were instructed to not consume any caffeinated drinks on the scanning day.
source: In addition, subjects were instructed to not consume any caffeinated drinks on the scanning day.
evidence: This describes a protocol restriction.

claim: fMRI scanning was performed after subjects consumed a standardized isocaloric dinner on the evening following the night of the sleep manipulation.
source: On the evening following the night of the sleep manipulation, fMRI scanning was performed after subjects consumed a standardized isocaloric dinner (subjects received exactly the same meal in both sessions).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Imaging data and blood samples were collected after dinner in the evening following the night of sleep manipulation because previous studies found that experimentally induced sleep deprivation affects ECS compounds and the desire for and consumption of energy-dense food most prominently in this time window.
source: We collected imaging data and blood samples after dinner in the evening following the night of sleep manipulation because previous studies found that experimentally induced sleep deprivation affects ECS compounds and the desire for and consumption of energy-dense food most prominently in this time window (Hanlon et al., 2016; Nedeltcheva et al., 2009).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the timing of data collection, supported by citations.

claim: During fMRI scanning, participants were presented with food odors, non-food odors, and clean air, and rated odor pleasantness and intensity.
source: During fMRI scanning, participants were presented with food odors, non-food odors, and clean air, and rated odor pleasantness and intensity.
evidence: This describes the fMRI task.

claim: Isocaloric meals were provided for the 24 hours preceding both fMRI sessions to equate food intake.
source: To equate food intake leading up to the two fMRI sessions, isocaloric meals were provided for the 24 hr preceding both sessions.
evidence: This describes the dietary control protocol.

claim: The study used an in-home setting to render the sleep-deprivation protocol as ecologically valid as possible.
source: Our study used an in-home setting to render the sleep-deprivation protocol as ecologically valid as possible without the additional distractions and stressors of being in an unfamiliar hospital laboratory environment.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the study design.

claim: In-home settings come with potential limitations related to non-compliance.
source: However, because in-home settings come with potential limitations related to non-compliance, we took several measures to reinforce and monitor compliance with the sleep stabilization and sleep manipulation schedule.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study design.

claim: Sleep and wake-up times were monitored for 8 days using wrist-worn 3-axis accelerometers.
source: Sleep and wake-up times were monitored for 8 days (7 days of stabilization, 1 day of manipulation) using a wrist-worn 3-axis accelerometers (ActiGraph GT9X Link, ActiGraph, LLC, Pensacola, FL) (Ancoli-Israel et al., 2003; Marino et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the monitoring method, supported by citations.

claim: Actigraphy data from two participants collected during the sleep stabilization phase of the NDS session was lost due to a technical failure.
source: Due to a technical failure, actigraphy data from two participants collected during the sleep stabilization phase of the NDS session was lost (data from both critical nights of sleep manipulation were not affected).
evidence: This describes missing data.

claim: Data from one additional participant recorded during one day of the sleep stabilization phase was also lost.
source: Data from one additional participant recorded during one day of the sleep stabilization phase was also lost.
evidence: This describes missing data.

claim: Actigraphy data were classified as sleep or awake using Cole-Kripke algorithm.
source: Actigraphy data were classified as sleep or awake using Cole-Kripke algorithm, as implemented in the Actilife software.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: Total sleep time, time in bed, sleep efficiency, and wake after sleep onset were calculated using the Cole-Kripke algorithm.
source: Total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TIB), sleep efficiency (SE), and wake after sleep onset (WASO) were also calculated using the same algorithm.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: Subjects logged their bed time, sleep duration, and sleep quality immediately after scheduled sleep hours in an online sleep diary.
source: In addition to wearing the actigraphy device, subjects also logged their bed time, sleep duration, and sleep quality immediately after scheduled sleep hours in an online sleep diary.
evidence: This describes the self-report monitoring method.

claim: Information entered in the sleep diary was time stamped, and study personnel cross-referenced these time stamps and entries with the actigraphy data.
source: Information entered in the sleep diary was time stamped, and study personnel cross-referenced these time stamps and entries with the actigraphy data.
evidence: This describes the compliance monitoring procedure.

claim: Participants who failed to follow the sleep protocol were excluded from the study.
source: Participants who failed to follow the sleep protocol were excluded from the study.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion.

claim: During the 24 hour period before each fMRI session, participants were provided with an isocaloric diet.
source: During the 24 hr period before each fMRI session, participants were provided with an isocaloric diet.
evidence: This describes the dietary control protocol.

claim: All meals were planned and packaged by a registered dietician at the Clinical Research Unit at Northwestern Memorial Hospital.
source: All meals were planned and packaged by a registered dietician at the Clinical Research Unit (CRU) at Northwestern Memorial Hospital
evidence: This describes the meal preparation procedure.

claim: Meals were based on individually estimated energy requirements according to height, weight, age, and sex.
source: and were based on individually estimated energy requirements according to height, weight, age, and sex.
evidence: This describes the meal planning procedure.

claim: Estimated calorie requirements ranged from 1400 to 2600 kcal/day.
source: Estimated calorie requirements ranged from 1400 to 2600 kcal/day.
evidence: This describes the range of calorie requirements.

claim: Meals were composed of 55–60% carbohydrate, 15–20% protein, and 25–30% fat.
source: Meals were composed of 55–60% carbohydrate, 15–20% protein, and 25–30% fat.
evidence: This describes the macronutrient composition of the meals.

claim: Participants were instructed to not consume any additional foods or drinks, other than water, during the 24 hour period preceding the fMRI session.
source: Participants were instructed to not consume any additional foods or drinks, other than water, during the 24 hr period preceding the fMRI session.
evidence: This describes a protocol restriction.

claim: Breakfast consisted of approximately 30% of total caloric needs.
source: Breakfast consisted of ~30% of total caloric needs
evidence: This describes the meal composition.

claim: Lunch and dinner each consisted of approximately 35% of the estimated calorie requirement.
source: while the lunch and dinner each consisted of ~35% of the estimated calorie requirement.
evidence: This describes the meal composition.

claim: The total calorie content of the standardized pre-scan dinner ranged from 490 to 910 kcal.
source: The total calorie content of this dinner ranged from 490 to 910 kcal (~35% of estimated calorie requirements)
evidence: This describes the dinner composition.

claim: The standardized pre-scan dinner was composed of 55–60% carbohydrate, 15–20% protein, and 25–30% fat.
source: and was composed of 55–60% carbohydrate, 15–20% protein, and 25–30% fat.
evidence: This describes the macronutrient composition of the dinner.

claim: All participants consumed the entire meal.
source: All participants consumed the entire meal.
evidence: This describes compliance with the protocol.

claim: For each participant, the same meals were provided in both fMRI sessions.
source: For each participant, the same meals were provided in both fMRI sessions.
evidence: This describes the within-subject control.

claim: All subjects reported that they did not consume any other foods or caffeinated and caloric drinks.
source: All subjects reported that they did not consume any other foods or caffeinated and caloric drinks.
evidence: This describes compliance with the protocol.

claim: Blood serum samples for ECS analysis were collected at 7:30 pm while subjects were inside the MRI scanner, 90 minutes after the initiation of dinner.
source: Blood serum samples for ECS analysis were only collected at 7:30 pm while subjects were inside the MRI scanner, 90 min after the initiation of dinner (in between the 2nd and 3rd fMRI run).
evidence: This describes the blood sampling protocol.

claim: Serum levels of 2-AG and 2-OG were quantified using chemical ionization liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry.
source: Serum samples were processed and the two compounds were quantified using chemical ionization liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS; Agilent LC-MSD 1100 series, Ramsey, MN), as previously described (Patel et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the assay method, supported by citation.

claim: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits were used for total plasma ghrelin and plasma leptin.
source: We used enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits for total plasma ghrelin (human ghrelin, Millipore), plasma leptin (human leptin, Millipore)
evidence: This describes the assay method.

claim: Cobas e411 analyzer was used for plasma insulin and serum cortisol.
source: and cobas e411 analyzer (Roche) for plasma insulin, and serum cortisol.
evidence: This describes the assay method.

claim: Subjects completed visual analogue scales to measure motivation to eat at baseline and at multiple time points after dinner.
source: On the day of fMRI scanning, subjects completed both paper and computerized versions of visual analogue scales to measure motivation to eat at baseline (before dinner) and 30 min, 60 min, 90 min, and 120 min after dinner initiation and after the ad libitum buffet (see below).
evidence: This describes the hunger assessment protocol.

claim: Sensation of hunger, fullness, satisfaction, and prospective food consumption was assessed at each timepoint.
source: At each timepoint, sensation of hunger, fullness, satisfaction, and prospective food consumption was assessed with following questions: (1) How hungry do you feel? (2) How full do you feel? (3) How satisfied do you feel? (4) How much do you think you can eat?
evidence: This describes the hunger assessment questions.

claim: After completion of the fMRI scan, participants were presented with excessive portion sizes of energy-dense sweet and savory food items in an all-you-can-eat buffet-style setting.
source: After completion of the fMRI scan, participants were presented with excessive portion sizes of energy-dense sweet (cinnamon roll, donut holes, chocolate chip cookies, mini muffins) and savory food items (hash browns, garlic bread, pizza bites, potato chips) in an all-you-can-eat buffet-style setting.
evidence: This describes the ad libitum buffet protocol.

claim: Participants were told that they could consume the food freely while they waited, if they wanted.
source: This waiting room contained the buffet of food options, and participants were told that they could consume the food freely while they waited, if they wanted.
evidence: This describes the buffet instructions.

claim: Food items were weighed before and after to determine the amount of food consumed.
source: Food items were weighed before and after to determine the amount of food consumed.
evidence: This describes the food intake measurement method.

claim: Total calorie and energy density of consumed food was calculated from the product nutrition labels.
source: Total calorie and energy density (kcal/g) of consumed food was calculated from the product nutrition labels.
evidence: This describes the calculation method.

claim: Participants were presented with identical buffet options in both testing sessions.
source: Participants were presented with identical buffet options in both testing sessions.
evidence: This describes the within-subject control.

claim: Participants were asked to record their food intake for 24 hours following the fMRI scan using a food diary to track food intake on the day following the experiment.
source: To track food intake on the day following the experiment (after a night of unrestricted sleep), participants were asked to record their food intake for 24 hr following the fMRI scan using a food diary.
evidence: This describes the next-day food intake tracking method.

claim: Nutritional information for each consumed food item was obtained from the United States Department of Agriculture Food Composition Databases.
source: To estimate total calories and fat consumed, nutritional information for each consumed food item was obtained from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food Composition Databases (ndb.nal.usda.gov/ndb/).
evidence: This describes the nutritional information source.

claim: During initial screening, participants rated the pleasantness of six energy-dense food odors in randomized order.
source: During initial screening, participants rated the pleasantness of six energy-dense food odors in randomized order (pot roast, potato chips, garlic bread, cinnamon roll, caramel, and gingerbread, provided by International Flavors and Fragrances [New York City, NY] and Kerry [Tralee, Ireland]).
evidence: This describes the odor selection procedure.

claim: Based on pleasantness ratings, two savory and two sweet odors were chosen for each participant such that they were matched in pleasantness.
source: Based on these ratings, two savory and two sweet odors were chosen for each participant such that they were matched in pleasantness, and these odors were used for the remainder of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the odor selection procedure.

claim: Edibility ratings for food and non-food odors collected during the screening session differed significantly between food and non-food odors.
source: Most importantly, edibility ratings for food and non-food odors collected during the screening session differed significantly between food and non-food odors (T24 = 12.69, p=3.87×10−12).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Odors were delivered directly to subjects' nose using a custom-built MR-compatible olfactometer.
source: For all odor ratings and the experimental task, odors were delivered directly to subjects' nose using a custom-built MR-compatible olfactometer (Howard and Kahnt, 2017; Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Suarez et al., 2019)
evidence: This describes the odor delivery method, supported by citations.

claim: The olfactometer is capable of redirecting medical grade air with precise timing at a constant flow rate of 3.2 L/min through the headspace of amber bottles containing liquid solutions of the odors.
source: capable of redirecting medical grade air with precise timing at a constant flow rate of 3.2 L/min through the headspace of amber bottles containing liquid solutions of the odors.
evidence: This describes the olfactometer specifications.

claim: At all times throughout the experiment, a constant stream of odorless air is delivered to participants' noses.
source: At all times throughout the experiment, a constant stream of odorless air is delivered to participants' noses, and odorized air is mixed into this airstream at specific time points, without changing in the overall flow rate.
evidence: This describes the odor delivery method.

claim: Odor presentation does not involve a change in somatosensory stimulation induced by the airstream.
source: Thus, odor presentation does not involve a change in somatosensory stimulation induced by the airstream.
evidence: Inferred from the constant flow rate design.

claim: All participants arrived at the scanning center after a 6 hour fast on the evening following the sleep manipulation.
source: On the evening following the sleep manipulation, all participants arrived at the scanning center after a 6 hr fast
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Each scanning session consisted of four fMRI runs.
source: Each scanning session consisted of four fMRI runs
evidence: This describes the fMRI protocol.

claim: Each run consisted of 63 pseudo-randomized trials of olfactory stimulation.
source: and each run consisted of 63 pseudo-randomized trials of olfactory stimulation.
evidence: This describes the fMRI task design.

claim: Each run consisted of nine presentations of the two sweet food odors, the two savory food odors, the two non-food control odors, and clean air.
source: Each run consisted of nine presentations of the two sweet food odors, the two savory food odors, the two non-food control odors, and clean air (totaling 63 trials/run).
evidence: This describes the fMRI task design.

claim: Functional MRI data were acquired on a Siemens 3T PRISMA system equipped with a 64-channel head-neck coil.
source: Functional MRI data were acquired on a Siemens 3T PRISMA system equipped with a 64-channel head-neck coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI scanner specifications.

claim: In each scanning run, 382 Echo-Planar Imaging volumes were acquired.
source: In each scanning run, 382 Echo-Planar Imaging (EPI) volumes were acquired with a parallel imaging sequence
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: A high-resolution T1-weighted structural scan was acquired at the beginning of the fMRI session.
source: A high-resolution (1 mm isotropic) T1-weighted structural scan was also acquired at the beginning of the fMRI session.
evidence: This describes the structural imaging protocol.

claim: Respiration was measured using a MR-compatible breathing belt affixed around the participant's torso.
source: Respiration, as an indirect measure of nasal sniffing, was measured using a MR-compatible breathing belt (BIOPAC Systems Inc, Goleta, CA) affixed around the participant's torso
evidence: This describes the respiratory monitoring method.

claim: Respiratory data was recorded at 1 kHz using PowerLab equipment.
source: and recorded at 1 kHz using PowerLab equipment (ADInstruments, Dunedin, New Zealand).
evidence: This describes the respiratory data acquisition.

claim: Pre-processing of fMRI data was performed using SPM12.
source: Pre-processing of fMRI data was performed using SPM12 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12/).
evidence: This describes the data analysis software.

claim: There were no sleep-dependent differences in head motion parameters.
source: There were no sleep-dependent differences in these composite head motion parameters (translation, T24 = 0.25, p=0.803; rotation, T24=−0.14, p=0.891).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of motion parameters.

claim: A searchlight-based multi-voxel pattern analysis was implemented to decode information about food vs. non-food odors.
source: We implemented a searchlight-based multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) (Howard and Kahnt, 2018; Kahnt et al., 2011) to decode information about food vs. non-food odors.
evidence: This describes the analysis method, supported by citations.

claim: The Decoding Toolbox was used to implement the searchlight.
source: We used The Decoding Toolbox (TDT) to implement the searchlight (Hebart et al., 2014)
evidence: This describes the analysis software, supported by citation.

claim: LIBSVM was used for the linear support vector machine classifier.
source: and LIBSVM (Chang and Lin, 2011) for the linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier.
evidence: This describes the analysis software, supported by citation.

claim: The generalized psycho-physiological interaction model was used to test for regions in which sleep-dependent changes in functional connectivity with the piriform cortex correlated with sleep-dependent changes in food intake.
source: We used the generalized psycho-physiological interaction (PPI) model (McLaren et al., 2012) to test for regions in which sleep-dependent changes in functional connectivity with the piriform cortex correlated with sleep-dependent changes in food intake.
evidence: This describes the connectivity analysis method, supported by citation.

claim: The seed region in the piriform cortex was defined from significant voxels in the contrast DS > NDS for decoding food vs. non-food odors.
source: The seed region in the piriform cortex was defined from significant voxels (p<0.001) in the contrast DS >NDS for decoding food vs. non-food odors.
evidence: This describes the seed region definition.
